title: Political influencer audiences do not simply mirror their parties: they combine stronger protest support with sharper doubts about institutional accountability
source_unit: Gallup and Charles F. Kettering Foundation analysis, What Podcaster Audiences Want From U.S. Democracy, June 15, 2026
geography: United States; adults in the 2025 Democracy for All / Kettering-Gallup study

observations.period: 2025 study; political news-source and audience frame

denominator.unit: more than 20,000 U.S. adults in the underlying Kettering-Gallup study; approximately 1,000 named a podcaster or influencer as a top news source

influencer_news_use.value: a small subgroup reported podcasters or online influencers among their core news sources

audience_grouping.value: audiences were grouped by the partisan identity of content creators' followers because most individual show samples were too small for separate reporting

party_nonidentity.value: influencer audiences diverged from broader partisan groups on several democratic-norm measures

observations.method: Secondary analysis of a large Kettering Foundation-Gallup U.S. adult study, with influencer audiences grouped by creator orientation and compared with party-affiliated respondents.
observations.uncertainty: The analysis is observational and the influencer subgroup is much smaller than the full sample; audience selection, creator exposure, political interest, and other differences are not causal estimates.
observations.subgroup: Adults naming left-leaning or right-leaning podcasters/influencers among top news sources, compared with Democrats or Republicans overall.
observations.counterinterpretation: Audience differences may reflect self-selection, age, education, political engagement, or content choice rather than influence by creators; creator-orientation grouping also compresses heterogeneous shows.

observations.period: 2025 study; support for peaceful protest and voting rights

denominator.unit: approximate U.S. adults in the underlying study naming a podcaster or influencer as a top news source; subgroup denominators vary by item

peaceful_protest_left_audience.unit: percent of left-leaning influencer audiences strongly agreeing that people with radical views should be able to protest peacefully, compared with 49 percent of Democrats overall

peaceful_protest_right_audience.unit: percent of right-leaning influencer audiences strongly agreeing, compared with 28 percent of Republicans overall

voting_rights.value: left-leaning influencer audiences were more supportive than their party peers of the right to vote for citizens with radical or uninformed views; the right-leaning audience showed little difference from Republicans overall

observations.method: Gallup comparison of democratic-principle responses across influencer-audience groups and party-affiliated respondents.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not establish why the groups differ, whether exposure preceded the attitude, or whether these attitudes translated into protest, voting, or other action.
observations.subgroup: Left-leaning and right-leaning influencer audiences, Democrats, Republicans, and respondents with differing views of political dissent.
observations.counterinterpretation: Influencer audiences may be more politically attentive or self-select into creators that match pre-existing commitments; stronger protest support can coexist with distrust of institutions.

observations.period: 2025 study; perceived accountability and civic efficacy

denominator.unit: approximate influencer-audience subgroup in the underlying Kettering-Gallup study; item-specific valid samples vary

leaders_accountability_left.unit: percent of left-leaning influencer audiences agreeing or strongly agreeing that political leaders will be held accountable, compared with 26 percent of Democrats

leaders_accountability_right.unit: percent of right-leaning influencer audiences agreeing or strongly agreeing, compared with 48 percent of Republicans

voting_effectiveness.value: 54 percent of left-leaning influencer audiences called voting very effective versus 49 percent of Democrats; 41 percent of right-leaning audiences did so versus 51 percent of Republicans

institutional_skepticism.value: both influencer-audience groups were more skeptical than their partisan peers that political leaders are held accountable

observations.method: Comparative descriptive analysis of accountability and voting-efficacy items in the Kettering-Gallup study.
observations.uncertainty: Perceived accountability and efficacy are judgments, not audited institutional performance or realized political influence; small subgroup differences may be imprecise.
observations.subgroup: Political influencer audiences and partisan comparison groups with different media environments and political identities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Skepticism may reflect greater attention to political conflict or a critical democratic stance rather than disengagement; confidence in voting is not turnout.

observations.period: 2025 study; protest efficacy and creator-specific contrasts

denominator.unit: approximate influencer-audience subgroup in the underlying study; named-show estimates are smaller

nonviolent_protest_left_audience.unit: percent of left-leaning influencer audiences saying nonviolent protest is very effective, compared with 22 percent of Democrats

named_show_contrast.value: 39 percent of MeidasTouch listeners called nonviolent protest very effective versus 10 percent of Joe Rogan listeners

political_route.value: creator-mediated news audiences may connect attention to a more action-oriented but institutionally skeptical political stance

observations.method: Gallup analysis of political-action efficacy items by influencer-audience orientation and selected named shows.
observations.uncertainty: Named-show comparisons have small samples and are not representative of all listeners; the analysis cannot separate creator content from audience selection or broader media ecosystems.
observations.subgroup: Listeners identifying selected political podcasters/influencers and broader left-leaning or right-leaning influencer audiences.
observations.counterinterpretation: A critical view of government accountability can motivate protest rather than withdrawal; stated efficacy does not establish event participation or policy change.

related_sources.claim: Pew-Knight supplies a separate public-life engagement typology linking news, civic activity, religion, and political participation.
Pew-Knight supplies a separate press-freedom and perceived media-influence route.

boundary: This record adds a U.S. media-to-politics route connecting influencer news use, democratic norms, protest and voting efficacy, accountability judgments, and institutional skepticism. It is a secondary analysis of a survey with small, selected influencer-audience subgroups; it does not establish creator causality, media exposure effects, actual political participation, persuasion, or institutional performance.
